drill_bank_notes: Seed set of 24 drills. Types: classify (multiple choice), produce (free text, AI-graded), rewrite (free text, AI-graded), spot (multiple choice), plan (free text, AI-graded). The app's drill-generator endpoint creates unlimited additional drills per concept_id using the playbook files as source context. Free-text drills are graded by the Claude grader prompt (see PROMPTS.md) returning score 1-4 mapped to FSRS ratings Again/Hard/Good/Easy.

drills.prompt: A referrer says: 'Tom always picks up, and if he says Friday, it's Friday.' Which trust equation component is this evidence of?
drills.explain: Doing what you say you'll do, consistently, over time = Reliability. Credibility is about whether your WORDS are believable; reliability is about your ACTIONS.

drills.prompt: In a first meeting, a grazier mentions his neighbour's bad refinance experience. You reply: 'That's exactly why our process is different — let me walk you through it.' What just happened?
options: Self-orientation spike: you made his story about you
drills.explain: You converted his disclosure into a pitch opportunity. The trusted-advisor move: explore HIS story first ('what happened to them?'). Pitching here raises S, the divisor that erodes everything.

drills.prompt: 'So if I'm hearing you right — the issue isn't really the rate, it's that nobody in the family can talk about what happens when your father steps back.' Which stage of the trust conversation is this?
drills.explain: Framing = crystallising the real issue cleanly and without blame, often naming what hasn't been said aloud. It follows listening and precedes envisioning the end state.

drills.prompt: Three minutes into a meeting, the client mentions cash-flow pressure at harvest. You immediately sketch an interest-only restructure. What's the error?
options: Premature solving: value of the solution wasn't built first
You should have quoted price first
drills.explain: Both Maister (skipping Listen/Frame/Envision) and Rackham (pitching before implied needs become explicit) name this the cardinal error. The same restructure lands 10x harder after implication and need-payoff questions.

drills.prompt: A client couple keep returning to 'the bank's fees are ridiculous' but mention, in passing, that the husband's brother is on the guarantee and they 'haven't seen him since Christmas.' Write one framing sentence that names what the real issue might be — without blame.
drills.grading_focus: Names the guarantee/family entanglement as the underlying issue; tentative not declarative ('it sounds like / I wonder if'); no blame assigned; invites confirmation.

drills.prompt: An accountant calls you about a client's succession problem two years before any finance need exists, saying 'I just wanted your read on this.' What relationship level does this indicate?
drills.explain: Being consulted on whatever matters, before any transaction exists, is the trust-based level — the safe haven for hard issues. This is the destination state for every priority referrer.

drills.prompt: 'If the working capital limit caps out mid-harvest again, what does that do to your ability to sell when the price is right rather than when cash forces you?' — classify this question.
drills.explain: It takes an established problem (limit capping out) and explores its consequences (forced selling, lost price optionality) — growing the problem's perceived seriousness. That's an implication question.

drills.prompt: 'How would it change the family conversation if the guarantees were restructured so your daughter could come into the business cleanly?' — classify this question.
drills.explain: It asks the client to articulate the VALUE of a solution — payoff, not pain. Need-payoff questions get the client persuading themselves.

drills.prompt: Problem stated by a Darling Downs cotton grower: 'Our bank takes six weeks to approve anything.' Write TWO implication questions that grow this problem's seriousness toward areas a refinance would solve.
drills.grading_focus: Questions explore consequences (missed land purchases, water entitlement opportunities, planting windows, counterparty confidence), not restatements of the problem; open not leading; client's world not product world.

drills.prompt: Same grower, after implications are developed. Write ONE need-payoff question that gets HIM to articulate what fast, pre-cleared credit appetite would be worth.
drills.grading_focus: Asks for value/usefulness in his words; future-positive framing; doesn't pitch Macquarie; specific to his operation.

drills.prompt: 'Honestly, the overdraft has been tight the last two seasons.' Implied or explicit need?
drills.explain: It expresses dissatisfaction, not a want. In large sales implied needs don't predict buying — your job is converting it to 'we need a facility that flexes with the season' via I and N questions.

drills.prompt: 'Macquarie can offer 12-month interest-only periods, which would solve the harvest squeeze you said is costing you your November selling position.' Feature, advantage, or benefit?
drills.explain: It links a capability to an EXPLICIT need this client stated. That strict linkage is what makes it a benefit — the only category that reliably drives success in large sales.

drills.prompt: Rewrite as a benefit, for a client who has said 'we can't plan anything because we never know where we stand with the bank': 'Macquarie provides annual review with a dedicated agri relationship manager.'
drills.grading_focus: Connects the capability to the stated explicit need (certainty/planning); uses the client's language; drops bank jargon.

drills.prompt: End of a referrer coffee: 'This was great — let's definitely stay in touch and grab lunch sometime.' Advance or continuation?
drills.explain: Warm words, no committed action. An advance would be: 'I'll send you the livestock seasonality benchmark Tuesday, and you'll introduce me to the Hartley file once you've cleared it with them.'

drills.prompt: You have a first meeting with a turnaround partner (Sarah Lindqvist profile) next week. Write your best-case advance and minimum-acceptable advance for the meeting.
drills.grading_focus: Both are specific committed actions with owners and timing; best-case is ambitious but realistic for a first meeting (e.g. a live file walkthrough); minimum still moves forward (e.g. agreed follow-up with a specific give).

drills.prompt: In roleplay, the client raised four price objections in ten minutes. Where did the seller most likely go wrong?
options: Pitched features/advantages before building need value
Client is just a price buyer
Should have handled objections more smoothly
drills.explain: Recurring price objections are usually seller-created: capabilities offered before the problem's seriousness outweighed the cost. Prevention (earlier I and N questions) beats handling.

drills.prompt: You mention that three cotton families on the Downs restructured the same way last season, and the client visibly relaxes. Which principle is at work?
drills.explain: Similar others' behaviour reducing uncertainty = social proof. The active ingredient is SIMILARITY — same region, commodity, scale. Generic case studies don't fire it.

drills.prompt: A young farming couple referred by their accountant asks if they should refinance now. Honest answer: their current deal is fine for another 18 months. Write your response — and note what it buys you.
drills.grading_focus: Clearly advises against own short-term interest; specific trigger to revisit (lease expiry, fixed-rate maturity); recognises the credibility/trust purchase and the referrer-protection effect.

drills.prompt: Which of these is ETHICAL scarcity? A) 'This rate is only on the table this week' (it isn't). B) 'Settling after March means you miss the winter-crop planting window — that's a real cost of waiting.' C) 'I have other clients keen on this structure.'
drills.explain: B frames a genuine, verifiable cost of delay as a loss. A is manufactured and relationship-fatal when discovered; C is vague pressure. The ethics test: does the lever point at a truth?

drills.prompt: Design a four-step micro-commitment ladder from 'interested grazier at a field day' to 'application lodged', where each step is small, active, and voluntary.
drills.grading_focus: Steps escalate gradually (e.g. send rate review docs -> meet with accountant -> family meeting attendance -> application); each is client-action not just seller-action; written confirmation noted.

drills.prompt: Rewrite so it contains zero criticism of people while still surfacing the problem: 'Whoever set up this structure made a mess — your old broker has cost you a fortune in unnecessary guarantees.'
drills.grading_focus: Critiques the structure not the person; assumes good faith ('made sense at the time'); preserves the client's pride in past decisions; still creates motivation to fix.

drills.prompt: You can see the right succession structure for the Brandt family. Write two questions that lead the family toward discovering the key element themselves, rather than you presenting it.
drills.grading_focus: Genuinely open questions that point at the insight without stating it; family does the concluding; no embedded pitch.

drills.prompt: Design this month's touch for a priority accountant referrer — with the constraint that it contains no ask of any kind. What do you send/do, and why does it land?
drills.grading_focus: Genuine value to THEM (intel, intro, client-back referral, relevant article with personal note, glue-based invite); zero ask; specific not generic; fits known relationship glue.

drills.prompt: Who is most likely the super-connector? A) A loyal client with one large property. B) A livestock agent who works saleyards across three regions. C) A credit analyst at a major bank. D) A solicitor who does only conveyancing.
drills.explain: Super-connectors have unusually LARGE and unusually DIVERSE networks. Agents, brokers-of-things, journalists, and industry-body figures sit at network crossroads. Invest disproportionately there.

drills.prompt: A Downs cotton grower says: 'We looked at switching two years ago and it was nothing but paperwork and broken promises.' Write the mirror — the one-to-three words you repeat back — and what you do immediately after.
drills.grading_focus: Mirrors the emotionally loaded tail words ('broken promises' or 'paperwork and broken promises'); upward inflection noted; followed by SILENCE, not a question or a defence of the industry.

drills.prompt: Rewrite as a Voss-style label: you want to acknowledge that a grazier feels disloyal even considering leaving his bank of 22 years. Your current draft: 'I understand loyalty is important to you, but our offer is significantly better.'
drills.grading_focus: Starts with 'It seems like / It sounds like / It feels like'; names the disloyalty/betrayal feeling specifically; NO 'but' and no pivot to the offer; ends with silence implied.

drills.prompt: First meeting with a senior turnaround partner who has been burned by brokers before. Write a three-item accusation audit to open with — the worst things she could be thinking about you.
drills.grading_focus: Items are genuinely the worst (commission-driven, won't last in the role, will embarrass her with clients); stated plainly without weaseling; no immediate self-defence after; invites her to confirm or correct.

drills.prompt: You summarise a matriarch's situation and she sighs: 'You're right.' What just happened?
options: Polite dismissal — she wants the conversation over; the summary didn't capture her world
She disagrees but won't say so
drills.explain: 'You're right' is social compliance — the conversational exit. The breakthrough is 'THAT'S right': your summary (facts + labelled emotion) captured her world so completely she endorses it as her own. Go back, listen more, summarise better.

drills.prompt: A rural accountant says he'll only refer you if you agree to co-brand all client communications under his firm's letterhead — which compliance won't allow. Write TWO calibrated (How/What) questions instead of saying no.
drills.grading_focus: Open How/What questions ('How am I supposed to get that past compliance?' / 'What's the problem co-branding solves for you?'); no flat refusal; puts the problem in his lap while keeping the relationship; surfaces the underlying need (credit/visibility with his clients).

drills.prompt: Your client just called: his bank matched your rate, waived fees, and gave him until Friday to fix. He sounds relieved and apologetic. Plan your response: the label, the two calibrated questions, and how you frame the deadline.
drills.grading_focus: Labels his relief/conflict and the bank's sudden attention WITHOUT criticising the bank; questions expose what matching the rate doesn't fix (structure, service, the next three years); deadline framed as the bank's pressure tactic vs his timeline; no panic discounting; secures an advance (e.g. side-by-side structure comparison before Friday).

drills.prompt: You must table indicative pricing first. Which opening is strongest? A) 'We can do 6.15%.' B) 'Facilities of this size and security profile are printing between 5.95% and 6.40% in the current market — where you land depends on the water entitlement treatment.' C) 'What rate would get this done?' D) 'We'll beat whatever your bank offers by 10 points.'
drills.explain: A range anchored to market data sets the frame without overcommitting, signals expertise, and makes the conversation about the drivers (structure, security) rather than a single haggling number. D races to the bottom and raises self-orientation; C surrenders the anchor.

drills.prompt: You've had two 'good' meetings with a grazing family but the deal feels stuck and you don't know why. Plan three concrete moves to surface the black swans — the unknown unknowns.
drills.grading_focus: Targets unguarded moments (arrive early / stay for the cuppa / the walk to the ute); asks no-oriented or calibrated questions about who else is affected; checks the guarantee/title web and the people NOT in the room; logs findings to the contact record.

drills.prompt: Build the one-sentence REFRAME for a corporate cotton CFO who believes debt is a commodity bought on price. It must teach him something counterintuitive about his own operation that you are distinctly placed to solve.
drills.grading_focus: Genuinely counterintuitive (e.g. execution certainty / committee risk costs more than margin at his scale); about HIS business not your product; quantifiable; leads back to a capability that differentiates you, not generic advice he can take to his incumbent.

drills.prompt: Third meeting. The couple agrees enthusiastically with everything, then asks to 'compare one more lender' — the same request as last meeting, different lender. What are you actually fighting?
options: The status quo — build more pain with implication questions
Indecision (fear of messing up) — stop adding value, start de-risking the decision
Lack of trust — go back to rapport building
drills.explain: Endless comparison-seeking plus agreement-without-commitment is the classic FOMU tell. More value arguments make it WORSE. Switch playbooks: recommendation, capped options, safety nets, smaller first step (JOLT).

drills.prompt: Rewrite for an indecisive couple drowning in options: 'So there's the fixed option, the variable option, a split, and we could also look at interest-only — what would you like to do?'
drills.grading_focus: ONE confident recommendation with the reasons anchored in THEIR stated situation; mentions at most one alternative; takes ownership ('in your position, here's what I'd do'); includes a de-risking element (review trigger, staged step); does not surrender the decision back to them undigested.

drills.prompt: The Vogels (profitable, obvious refinance case, paralysed by their mistimed dairy exit) need the decision de-risked, not re-sold. Design the start-small path and two safety nets you'd put on the table.
drills.grading_focus: Start-small is a real commitment that builds consistency (e.g. refinance the working-capital facility only, term debt at review); safety nets are explicit and honest (pre-approval before any application, defined exit/review points, worst-realistic-case named); no new value arguments piled on; acknowledges the dairy-exit scar without dwelling.
